doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: Charlie Fowlkes's death and the show must go on
summary: Baritonist Charlie Fowlkes died on the bus; the band played that night.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: You know getting back to that story about Charlie Fowlkes, it’s not a pleasant one unfortunately, but about the show must go on concept that Basie had. Charlie Fowlkes went to sleep on the band bus just like this, and had a massive heart attack. And he was a big man, he was over 320 pounds. And he bet me one hundred dollars that he could lose 30 pounds before I did. And it was just like a week ago before that that we made that bet. And it took almost ten people to lift him off the bus. And it was very strange. But you know what? Three hours later, we were on stage playing, and people were dancing right up to Basie and Basie is smiling and joking with the crowd. I was totally stunned, but I couldn’t believe I was playing the drums. But you know what? Out of respect to Charlie Fowlkes’ memory and to the respect and dignity of Count Basie’s memory and everything, we got on the bandstand and we played. And Count was an amazing man. He got me through that night you know. And I learned so much about the show must go on. Because in many ways you may not feel like getting up there on a few occasions. You might be depressed emotionally or feeling a little under the weather physically or something. But there’s something about getting on that stage and when the curtain opens, that’s what heals your soul and that’s what makes you who you are and separates the men from the boys or the ladies from the girls or whatever. But the main thing is play, and dedicate your life to the love of the groove, and help people to feel that joyous feeling. And that’s what I think my whole dedication is all about.
That’s marvelous. And you know I was going to say as we wrap up here, if you have some words for our students — I think you just said them.
